lead: A graph colouring assigns a colour to each vertex so that neighbours get different colours. This models any situation where linked items must be kept apart: exams that share a student, variables live at the same time, or radio transmitters that interfere. The chromatic number χ(G) is the smallest number of colours that works. It measures the true conflict in the graph, not just its size. Scheduling rooms, allocating registers in a compiler and colouring maps all use this one idea.
prereq: You need: graph vocabulary and adjacency from 6.1, and the planar bound from 6.5.

blocks.text: A proper vertex colouring of a graph G = (V, E) gives every vertex a colour so that for each edge uv the colours of u and v differ. The graph is k-colourable if such a colouring uses at most k colours; unused colours are allowed. The chromatic number χ(G) is the least k for which G is k-colourable.
χ(G) = min { k ≥ 1 : G is k-colourable }
blocks.where: χ(G) is the chromatic number of G; k is a positive integer; G is k-colourable when a proper colouring with at most k colours exists.

blocks.text: A colour class is all vertices with one colour. No edge can lie inside a colour class, so each class is an independent set. A k-colouring splits V into k independent sets.
A graph with no edges and at least one vertex has χ = 1. The complete graph K_n has χ = n, because every pair of vertices is adjacent and all n colours must be distinct.

A clique is a set of vertices that are all pairwise adjacent. Its size is at most the number of colours, since clique vertices must all receive different colours. So χ(G) ≥ ω(G), where ω(G) is the clique number, the largest clique size. The triangle A, B, C in the figure has size 3, so at least 3 colours are needed.

items: Order the vertices v1, v2, ..., vn.
For each later vertex vi, look at its already coloured neighbours and give vi the smallest positive integer not used on those neighbours.
Continue until every vertex has a colour.

blocks.text: After each step the colouring stays proper. A vertex has at most Δ(G) neighbours, where Δ(G) is the maximum degree. Those neighbours block at most Δ(G) colours, so one of Δ(G)+1 colours is always free. Therefore χ(G) ≤ Δ(G)+1. The bound is often loose; C5 has Δ = 2 and χ = 3.

A graph is bipartite exactly when it is 2-colourable exactly when it has no odd cycle. The two bipartition classes give colours 1 and 2. An odd cycle cannot alternate two colours and close. If there is no odd cycle, a breadth-first search from any vertex assigns alternating colours.
The four colour theorem says every simple planar graph is 4-colourable. K4 is planar and needs 4, so the number cannot be lowered.

Map colouring treats each region as a vertex; an edge joins regions with a shared border. The four colour theorem guarantees four colours for a planar map. The theorem covers planar graphs, not all graphs: K5 needs 5 colours.

Exam scheduling builds a graph with exams as vertices. An edge joins two exams that share a student. A colour is a time slot, and a proper colouring puts conflicting exams in different slots. The chromatic number is the minimum number of slots. The same model assigns channels to mobile towers that interfere, or rooms to classes that cannot run together.

A compiler's register allocator builds a graph of variables. An edge joins two variables live at the same time. Colours are CPU registers; χ is the minimum registers needed. If too few registers exist, some variables spill to memory.
Only a few syllabi add the chromatic polynomial P_G(k), which counts proper colourings with k colours.

figure.caption: The triangle A-B-C forces three colours; the shown proper colouring uses colour 1 for A and D, colour 2 for B and E, and colour 3 for C.

spec.aria: A five-vertex graph with cycle A B C D E A and chord A C, coloured with 3 colours; triangle A B C forces at least 3 colours.

examples.question: For the graph with vertices A, B, C, D, E and edges AB, BC, CD, DE, EA, AC, find χ and give a proper 3-colouring.
steps: Write V = {A, B, C, D, E}. The edges are AB, BC, CD, DE, EA and AC. Degrees: deg(A) = 3, deg(B) = 2, deg(C) = 3, deg(D) = 2, deg(E) = 2, so Δ(G) = 3.

The vertices A, B, C form a triangle: AB, BC and AC are all edges. A triangle is a clique of size 3, so ω(G) ≥ 3 and χ(G) ≥ 3. A K4 would need four vertices each of degree at least 3; only A and C have degree 3, so no K4 exists and ω(G) = 3.
Try 3 colours. Set colour(A) = 1, colour(B) = 2, colour(C) = 3. Set colour(D) = 1, which is allowed because D's neighbours are C and E. Set colour(E) = 2.
Check all edges: AB gives 1 and 2; BC gives 2 and 3; CD gives 3 and 1; DE gives 1 and 2; EA gives 2 and 1; AC gives 1 and 3. All differ, so this is a proper 3-colouring and χ(G) ≤ 3.
The triangle proves χ(G) ≥ 3, and the colouring proves χ(G) ≤ 3. Hence χ(G) = 3.
examples.answer: χ(G) = 3 colours; one proper colouring is (A, B, C, D, E) = (1, 2, 3, 1, 2).

traps: χ(G) is not Δ(G)+1 in general. The greedy bound χ ≤ Δ+1 can be loose; find a colouring and a lower bound before writing equality.
A graph with no triangle can still need 3 colours. C5 is triangle-free (ω = 2) but χ(C5) = 3; bipartite graphs are exactly the 2-colourable graphs with no odd cycle.
'k-colourable' means at most k colours, not exactly k. An empty graph is 3-colourable but has χ = 1.
The four colour theorem applies to simple planar graphs, not to every graph. K5 is non-planar and needs 5 colours.

quiz.q: Define a proper vertex colouring and the chromatic number χ(G).
quiz.a: A proper vertex colouring gives each vertex a colour so that adjacent vertices have different colours. χ(G) is the least number of colours needed for a proper colouring of G.

quiz.q: Why does a triangle force at least three colours?
quiz.a: In a triangle every pair of the three vertices is adjacent. Each vertex must differ from the other two. Two colours would have to repeat on two adjacent vertices, so three distinct colours are necessary.

quiz.q: Find χ(C5), the cycle on five vertices.
quiz.a: C5 is an odd cycle, so it is not bipartite and not 2-colourable. A 3-colouring is possible by alternating two colours around four vertices and giving the last vertex the third colour. Hence χ(C5) = 3.

quiz.q: A graph has maximum degree Δ = 4. What does the greedy bound guarantee, and is χ necessarily 5?
quiz.a: The greedy algorithm guarantees χ ≤ Δ + 1 = 5. The value χ is not necessarily 5; it may be smaller. The bound is only an upper guarantee.

quiz.q: A graph has no triangle. Must it be 2-colourable? Justify your answer.
quiz.a: No. A triangle-free graph can have an odd cycle of length 5 or more. C5 is triangle-free but contains a 5-cycle, so it is not bipartite and χ(C5) = 3. A graph is 2-colourable exactly when it has no odd cycle, not when it has no triangle.

quiz.q: State the four colour theorem and explain why K4 shows that four colours are sometimes necessary.
quiz.a: Every simple planar graph is 4-colourable. K4 is planar. In K4 every pair of the four vertices is adjacent, so all four vertices need different colours. Thus K4 needs exactly four colours.

beyond: Not for the exam. Graph colouring continues in compiler design, wireless network planning and exam timetabling software. Researchers study edge colouring, list colouring and colouring of hypergraphs. The Lovasz Local Lemma gives existence proofs for some hard colouring problems. Search terms: chromatic polynomial, register allocation by graph colouring, hypergraph colouring.
